channel.title: Veille IA & maths — daily digest
channel.description: Daily summary of Xena, Proofs and Prompts, Silicon Reckoner, Tao (blog and Mastodon) and Gowers.

item.title: Digest — 12 November 2026 (5 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from: Timothy Gowers, Terence Tao (Mastodon).

Xena (Kevin Buzzard) — “…and the proof is checked in Lean”

  • Buzzard explains what "verified in Lean" really guarantees, especially for AI-generated code, as four checks: does the Lean statement match the paper; does it compile; does the proof prove that exact statement; does it rely on a kernel bug.
  • On statements: he notes that roughly 38 of the 290 OpenAI theorem-dump papers with Lean code do not even state the main theorem. Paper 194 (Lech's conjecture) only formalises Corollary 5.4. Axiom's finite-simple-groups classification depends on about 5,600 lines of unchecked definitions in the AI-written Tau Ceti library.
  • Tools: lake comparator checks that the proved theorem matches a trusted statement and uses only standard axioms. Its --paranoid mode re-checks with several independent kernels, one of them formally verified.
  • Anecdotes: compiling Anthropic's 13M-line FLT formalisation took a 96-core, 500 GB machine. OpenAI's Navier–Stokes proof (640K lines) builds on his laptop. A compiled Lean proof still says nothing about whether the PDF is correct.
  • 👉 A clear checklist to use whenever someone says an AI result is "checked in Lean".

Xena (guest post) — A Modern Reorganization of Mathematics

  • A guest post by Bin Dong, Nailin Guan, Jiedong Jiang, Ruochuan Liu, Christian Merten, Xiangyu Pan, Tingxiao Shi, Bin Wu, Edison Xie and Wei Yang. It argues that mathematics has two layers, intuition and slogans versus rigorous detail, and that AI can finally connect them.
  • Prototype: a complete, layered proof of the Weil conjectures on a website. A reader can start from the top-level strategy (Weil cohomology, ℓ-adic cohomology, six operations on the pro-étale site) and drill down to nodes linked to machine-checked Lean proofs.
  • Division of labour: humans choose the proof route and the key definitions, and formalised derived categories and the six-functor formalism by hand (building on Riou's work). LLMs refine the middle layers, and auto-formalisation does the bottom layer.
  • They picture it growing like the Stacks Project, for example with perverse sheaves and nearby/vanishing cycles.
  • 👉 Worth reading in full: a concrete model of AI-assisted exposition in algebraic geometry.

Terence Tao — Lean Grimoire

  • With a coding agent, Tao rebuilt his 2018 JavaScript logic textbook "QED". It teaches propositional and first-order logic as a crafting game where you apply inference rules to reach a goal.
  • New features include an optional live view of the matching in-progress Lean proof, and a playful "fantasy mode" where statements become potions and expressions become scrolls.
  • He is asking for playtesters, to make it more useful for teaching proofs and Lean.

Proofs and Prompts (Filip Dul) — Mathematics as a spiritual endeavor

  • A Hartford assistant professor argues that the AI turmoil only threatens a mathematics defined by problem-solving, which he sees as a recent, roughly century-old emphasis.
  • For him the core is awe and shared understanding: his own examples are Gauss–Bonnet, homotopy invariance and general relativity. Teaching passes that on.
  • Even if machines found every truth, he says mathematicians would remain their "stewards" and explainers.

Proofs and Prompts (anonymous postdoc) — On the great hypocrisy behind « human understanding »

  • A polemical essay, framed by Grothendieck's Récoltes et Semailles. The author argues that senior mathematicians' new praise of "human understanding" hides an academic system that has long rewarded conjecture-solving, publication counts and patronage.
  • Diagnosis: conjectures were already "Goodharted" into career metrics, and quick 30-minute journal reviews push out conceptual work. Shrinking resources select for technical, unoriginal profiles, which are the ones AI now hurts most.
  • The author mocks the techno-optimist, moralist and doomer camps alike, and condemns today's rush to have AI one-shot famous conjectures for arXiv. They also note that there is no guidance yet for this hiring season.
  • The author is leaving academia but will keep doing mathematics for pleasure. They suggest using AI as a Socratic partner to build understanding.
  • 👉 A sharp junior view on hiring, journals and supervision responsibilities, with many French references.

item.title: Digest — 11 November 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from: Xena (Kevin Buzzard), Timothy Gowers.

Proofs and Prompts (Antonio E. Porreca) — Why we should reject AI in academia

  • A maître de conférences at Aix-Marseille argues that AI-generated papers, prompted by OpenAI's release of 722 such "papers" vetted by an advisory group (AGMAI), should not be treated as legitimate research.
  • His case: these texts ignore academic norms (citing, not scooping, collaborating, writing in good faith), and researchers have a right, even a duty, not to cite or referee them.
  • Main worry is the pipeline: if students and juniors lean on LLMs, no new experts will form, and current experts will lose their skills over time.
  • He also calls on colleagues doing research on generative LLMs to switch fields.
  • 👉 A sharp anti-AI position from inside the French community, with direct points about students and PhD training.

Proofs and Prompts (Jonathan Noel) — I’m giving my theorems away

  • Noel (Victoria) describes a wasteful race: many people get the same AI proof of an open problem, keep it secret, and rush to post it on arXiv first.
  • He traces this to three habits: publishing only polished drafts, treating co-authorship as sacred, and always crediting whoever generated the proof.
  • His experiment, proofsandpeople.org, lists AI-generated proofs not yet understood by humans as open "projects" with a leader and a team who digest them and write them up with shared credit. He seeded it with 10 projects and is giving 8 of them away.
  • He also has a cost reason: he dropped from a $200 to a $20 ChatGPT plan. Links to related essays by Litt, Kra, Trombetti and Morris.

Proofs and Prompts (Carla Cederbaum) — Quo vadis, Mathematics?

  • A Tübingen differential geometer (mathematical relativity) argues that human-to-human mentoring, feedback and peer support are what the AI debate overlooks.
  • Practical ideas: students defend homework orally in front of a TA, "ask a human first" study rooms, more interactive classes, and local panels on when AI use helps learning.
  • She also asks mathematicians to explain publicly why mathematics and trained mathematicians matter, partly to protect teaching and research funding. Also published in the DMV Mitteilungen.
  • 👉 Useful concrete ideas for teaching and PhD supervision.

Terence Tao — “Six Math Essentials” now available (also on Mastodon)

  • Tao's popular mathematics book is now out in print, digital and audiobook formats.
  • The post gathers reviews (New Scientist, Publishers Weekly, Library Journal), an excerpt with a podcast on Science Friday, and interviews with Numberphile and Big Think.

item.title: Digest — 10 November 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from: Xena (Kevin Buzzard), Timothy Gowers, Terence Tao on Mastodon.

Proofs and Prompts (Juan Souto) — If Life Gives You Lemons…

  • A deliberately colloquial anti-doom rant (originally an e-mail, written without AI) by a CNRS directeur de recherche at IRMAR, Rennes: the panic among mathematicians mixes up separate questions (jobs, devalued papers, students, fun) that should be pulled apart.
  • Jobs: mathematicians are funded for teaching and for the occasional economically valuable spin-off, not cultural prestige; a faster research tool is an argument for more funding, and the real risk is mathematicians loudly declaring the field over.
  • Hiring must stop counting papers, but a week of talking to two people still reveals who is the better mathematician. PhD topics of the "solid problem that surely yields something" type are now five-minute AI tasks, so he admits he would not know what to give a new student.
  • His own practice: think as if AI didn't exist, then let it "break stones" on the painful lemma once he understands why it holds. His main worry is that the community stops sharing open questions, now that "questions are the new gold".
  • 👉 A French voice speaking directly to PhD supervision and to anxious postdocs (MPI, IHES and the rest will keep hiring for now).

Proofs and Prompts (Senthil Rajasekaran) — The Bigger Picture

  • A TCS postdoc (ULB) whose conceptual, definition-driven style should make him the most welcoming of theorem-provers argues that mathematics was not singled out but was a convenient "target of opportunity" for demonstrating AGI-style capabilities.
  • He calls it a hostile move: the goal of AI companies is replacing human labour at scale, not augmenting it, and mathematicians should ally with translators, artists and laid-off workers rather than seek special sympathy.
  • Ends with an explicitly political call to defend the meaning of human effort before trying to "take back control" of the field.

Proofs and Prompts (Antonio Lerario) — The shape of mathematical knowledge

  • A SISSA professor's philosophical essay built on three principles: science should serve human life; AI contributions should be judged on their merits rather than excluded for being artificial; human participation should be kept as a deliberate choice.
  • Main proposal: a shared, persistent "epistemic object", a layered hypergraph with a formalized core (definitions, proofs, dependencies, provenance) plus semantic layers for explanation, with Stacks Project, Verso Blueprint, MathHub and TheoremGraph cited as predecessors. It would pay off the corpus's accumulated "epistemic debt" and keep a flood of new results usable.
  • Research would be organised into long collective programmes that outlive their founders. Education should find the formative difficulties worth preserving, and evaluation should reward exposition, connections and good questions over priority and "theorem ownership". He also suggests departments run local models.
  • 👉 Worth reading in full: a constructive structural vision rather than a reaction piece.

Terence Tao (guest post) — Our Survey of Early Career Mathematicians

  • Anna Brandenberger, Hanna Mularczyk and Dora Woodruff (MIT) present an informal survey of over 260 grad students and postdocs from about 60 institutions on AI, with results posted on the arXiv on 29 October.
  • The authors highlight the questions on career outlook and research motivation as the most striking, and note that most responses predate 6 October, so opinion may have shifted since.
  • They urge journals, hiring committees and faculty to take junior voices into account.
  • 👉 Relevant for PhD supervision: the post itself is short, but the linked results are the substance.

item.title: Digest — 9 November 2026 (3 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from Xena (Kevin Buzzard), Timothy Gowers or Terence Tao on Mastodon.

Proofs and Prompts (Filippo A. E. Nuccio) — Formalisation as a concrete manifestation of mathematical understanding

  • A Mathlib maintainer (Université Saint-Étienne) argues that formalising mathematics by hand is a way to turn the vague notion of "understanding" into a tangible, checkable scientific output, largely independent of AI.
  • He draws a parallel with open access: blaming publishers (or AI companies) is a distraction when the community's own reward system (publication counts, rankings) undervalues time spent understanding.
  • Formalising is not mechanical: it means recasting definitions and proofs into better-suited forms, a collective effort (Mathlib, ~2.5M lines, hundreds of contributors); he cites the aims of the Annals of Formalized Mathematics, which he co-founded with Rob Lewis.
  • Autoformalisation by LLMs is to human-built libraries what bookbinding is to the printing press: it relies on Mathlib rather than replacing it. Refers to Gowers' recent text on the many purposes of mathematics.
  • 👉 French mathematical community voice (also active in MathOA and the French Committee for Open Science); relevant to how to frame PhD students' work.

Terence Tao (guest post: Jana Gevertz & Steffen Marcus) — What should we teach our (undergraduate) students?

  • Follow-up to Lozano-Robledo's "what should we tell our students?": two faculty at a New Jersey liberal arts college ask how undergraduate curricula should change now that AI turns advanced coursework into a push-button exercise.
  • Core tension: understanding comes from productive struggle (e.g. finding the right substitution yourself), yet students must learn to check and interpret AI output; both "ban it" and "rebuild everything around it" are rejected.
  • They pose open questions: more emphasis on conceptual reasoning and modelling (per the MAA statement on AI), critical evaluation of AI output, Lean in proof-based courses, fewer topics, coordination with other disciplines; and call for AMS/MAA leadership and federal grants.

Proofs and Prompts (Sajad Ahmad Sheikh) — Sisyphus and the Sorcerer: An Existential Meditation at the Chalkboard

  • A personal essay (University of Kashmir) recasting Camus' Sisyphus: mathematicians once formed a village whose stones stayed up; AI is a "sorcerer" (a golem we built) lifting ever-heavier stones.
  • Past shocks (Gödel, the four-colour proof, the classification of finite simple groups) kept understanding with humans; the worry now, following Thurston, is whether anyone will be able to say why a theorem is true.
  • He questions the usual reassurances (humans will choose the questions; maths as a hobby like chess) and names the new threat as superfluity rather than futility, ending on an honest "not proven".

item.title: Digest — 8 November 2026 (2 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from Xena (Kevin Buzzard), Timothy Gowers, Terence Tao's blog or Terence Tao on Mastodon.

Proofs and Prompts (Yifu Zhang) — On Expositions, and the Navier–Stokes Generation of PhD Students

  • A first-year numerical analysis PhD student at Imperial describes starting a doctorate right after this year's Navier–Stokes episode, alongside AI results on the Crouzeix conjecture and on matrix-multiplication complexity, and the career anxieties that come with it.
  • A small chart of blog posts by professional mathematicians suggests AI discussion has grown while expository writing has not, despite all the talk about the value of human understanding.
  • Argues for promoting casual, quirky exposition, with Littlewood's A Mathematician's Miscellany as the model: it makes hard mathematics accessible to newcomers, points readers to good sources, supports outreach, and shows junior researchers the field is still alive beyond AI.
  • 👉 A useful view of how incoming PhD students feel this year; relevant to supervision.

Proofs and Prompts (Reuven Peleg) — What Mathematicians Want?

  • A Hebrew University CS master's student notes that the debate so far has been reactive (whether to work with the labs, how journals should treat AI papers) and asks instead what mathematicians actually want from AI.
  • Sketches two camps: those who want AI limited to literature search, spellchecking and coding help, and those who welcome machine-discovered mathematics once reliability, attribution and responsibility are settled.
  • Short post that ends with an open call for mathematicians to describe their ideal outcome, so that AI-for-math researchers build something useful.

item.title: Digest — 7 November 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from Xena (Kevin Buzzard), Timothy Gowers or Terence Tao on Mastodon.

Proofs and Prompts (Nihar Gargava) — It's a great time to be an amateur mathematician

  • A Paris-Saclay postdoc reflects on outsiders producing real results with AI. Opening story (told by Dinesh Thakur at a TIFR "AI for Math" meeting): a French car mechanic, who didn't know what a finite field was, used Claude to disprove a Thakur conjecture on Carlitz–Wieferich primes (arXiv:2607.15305).
  • His own "Ramanujan–Hardy moment": Michael Simkin, an ex-IMO medallist and Game of Life constructor with no university training, sent him a messy AI write-up giving a new lower bound for lattice sphere packings in high dimensions. It became a joint paper with a PhD student (arXiv:2610.12619).
  • Argues that professionals should engage with some of these hobbyists as a form of outreach. He advises hobbyists to learn how mathematicians actually communicate, and professionals to respect hobbyists' ambitions.
  • 👉 Paris-based author; a concrete model for handling the AI-assisted "outsider" emails that are becoming common.

Proofs and Prompts (Chenmin Sun) — Nothing More than Tools?

  • A CNRS PDE researcher (UPEC) describes his journey from treating LLMs as cheap helpers to an "existential crisis", triggered by GPT-5.6 and by OpenAI's 6 October release of manuscripts grouped into 372 result families.
  • Criticises the addictive practice of "drawing cards" on open problems with agent swarms, and asks who deserves authorship when the work comes from nearly context-free prompting.
  • His answer is "toolization": the model handles bounded local tasks (estimates, numerics, case checks, learning other fields), while the human steers the key choices: blow-up profiles, ansätze, norms, Lyapunov functionals. If the model supplies a key idea, he would credit it as a collaborator.
  • Suggests regular self-checks against deskilling, e.g. whether he can still do AI-free mathematics on a plane.

Proofs and Prompts (Alessio Figalli, Sobhan Seyfaddini) — Postdoc Hiring in the Age of AI: What Still Matters

  • Two ETH professors, first entry in a series of advice from hiring committees: AI does not change the goal, which is to judge depth of understanding, the candidate's own contribution and potential.
  • Publication counts are not a reliable signal; letters, CVs and a close reading of selected papers matter for shortlisting. The interview (a talk plus in-depth discussion of what failed and why the arguments work) is decisive.
  • 👉 Directly useful when advising your PhD students on postdoc applications this season.

Terence Tao — More posts

  • A short list of further essays on AI and mathematics: Pavel Etingof's guide for young mathematicians on using AI in research, two pieces by Anna Gilbert, one by Larry Guth, and one by Atoosa Kasirzadeh. Readers are invited to add links in the comments.
  • 👉 Etingof's guide for young mathematicians looks worth passing to students.

item.title: Digest — 6 November 2026 (2 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from Xena (Kevin Buzzard), Timothy Gowers or Terence Tao on Mastodon.

Proofs and Prompts (Francesco Fournier-Facio, Yara Kyrychenko, Jon Roozenbeek, Julian Wykowski) — Futures of Maths Launch (also on Tao's blog)

  • Launch of Futures of Maths, an ongoing online consultation asking active research mathematicians how AI is changing their research and teaching, and where the field is heading.
  • Participants rate short statements on maths and AI on an agree/disagree scale, flag the ones they consider most important, see aggregate ratings afterwards, and can submit their own (moderated) statements, so the question set evolves.
  • Eligibility: at least one zbMATH-indexed journal article in the last five years, checked via ORCID/Crossref (or a manual review by institutional email). Verification is kept separate so the survey stays anonymous; you get a personal return link that cannot be resent.
  • Results will be published on Proofs and Prompts once enough responses are in; the organisers ask for wide and diverse participation.
  • 👉 You qualify as a participant, and it takes only a few minutes; worth passing on to colleagues and students in Paris too.

Proofs and Prompts (anonymous math PhD student) — I'm Not Done Doing Math! Don't Ignore Me!

  • Part of the series on publishing and credit. The author, a soon-to-graduate PhD with no papers and no research-postdoc prospects, argues that AI makes it realistic to keep doing research alongside a teaching load or a day job.
  • Main complaint: both pro- and anti-AI voices on the blog ignore people outside research positions; summits and society norm-setting are run by already successful mathematicians.
  • Pushes back on several proposals: if referees are scarce, the many PhDs who leave academia could review; replacing papers with seminars and workshops would exclude those without travel funding; fears of maths becoming a "hobby" ignore decades of a brutal job market.
  • 👉 A useful perspective for PhD supervision: what research life after a weaker PhD might look like with AI tools.

item.title: Digest — 5 November 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from Xena (Kevin Buzzard), Timothy Gowers or Terence Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao — More of my interviews and talks

  • A reference list of Tao's recent media pieces on maths and AI. He notes that most posts on his blog are now guest posts, and that his own views are collected on a separate page.
  • Highlights: a Nature World View op-ed calling for a "Maths 2.0" (22 Oct), an Observer interview (23 Oct), Science Friday (28 Oct), a New Scientist piece on the AI race to solve a famous problem (28 Oct), and Rivka Galchen's New Yorker feature "The Year Math Changed Forever" (1 Nov).
  • Also a SAIR Foundation conversation with Yu Deng on open math models. Tao discloses that some of this press is tied to his new book, out on 10 November.
  • 👉 The Nature op-ed and the New Yorker piece are the most substantial if you want his current position in full.

Proofs and Prompts (Anonymous postdoc) — Reject the Neurosis, and Terrible Messaging, of our Loudest Voices — The Case for (Ir)rational Optimism

  • A plea to senior mathematicians to tone down apocalyptic statements to the press. The author argues that this rhetoric is poor leadership and is seriously hurting the morale of PhD students and postdocs.
  • Argues that AI will push the field away from prestige-laden classical conjectures, which the author welcomes. It will also flood the literature with incremental "slop" papers and make papers a weaker signal of ability.
  • Hopes evaluation will shift towards chalk talks, exams and conversation, and that a PhD will again certify the ability to teach core undergraduate and graduate courses.
  • 👉 Relevant to PhD supervision and to how seniors talk to students about AI.

Proofs and Prompts (Anna Maltsev) — In Defence of Incremental Mathematics

  • Part of the series on publishing and credit. A random-matrix probabilist (QMUL) argues that incremental work is the brickwork that breakthroughs need, using the Ricci-flow results that led to Perelman as her example. She adds that it is how early-career people get trained and credited.
  • She reports being two to three times more productive with ChatGPT, and expects the volume of papers to grow by the same factor.
  • Proposal, first raised at the Royal Society AI meeting: split top journals into a flagship plus five online "daughter" journals, on the Nature model, and pay referees £100 per report, with AI checking the routine correctness.
  • An AI-generated cost estimate gives about £2.1M a year (plus £0.5M to launch) for ten journal families, including Annals, Inventiones, Publ. IHÉS and Ann. ENS. Her stance: "Keep calm and carry on", reinforce the system rather than tear it down.

Proofs and Prompts (Joachim von zur Gathen) — Picasso rephrased: AI is useless

  • A very short note built on a (possibly apocryphal) Picasso line: computers only give answers.
  • Its point is that OpenAI's 6 October post attacks the open problems that have guided mathematics. The open question is whether AI will ever pose new problems as fruitful as the old ones.

item.title: Digest — 4 November 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from Xena (Kevin Buzzard), Timothy Gowers or Terence Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao — Doctoral Advising Guidelines by the AHM

  • A guest post by the AHM communications group, reposting the announcement already covered yesterday from Proofs and Prompts.
  • It points to the Association for Human Mathematics' five recommendations on doctoral advising: human-authored writing, limits on reliance on AI, the ethics of AI use, and student wellbeing.
  • Now that it is on Tao's blog, it will reach a much wider audience, and the comments there may be worth a look.

Proofs and Prompts (Marco Trombetti) — Keeping Mathematical Conferences Human

  • Argument: AI makes polished slides, scripts and ready-made answers cheap, but understanding is not getting cheaper. A smooth talk therefore says less and less about whether the speaker understands the work.
  • Proposal: talks as an interview. A chair reads the paper beforehand and keeps interrupting (why this definition, where is the hard step, what is the simplest example), and the audience can join in throughout.
  • He takes the stress objection seriously, especially for junior speakers and non-native English speakers. Possible fixes: questions shared in advance, questions that explain rather than attack, and keeping classic talks as an option.
  • Bigger picture: conferences as a soft stage of "humanization" and verification, where someone has to sit beside a result and discuss it. He suggests trying one session of five speakers before changing anything more widely.
  • 👉 A concrete, testable idea that a seminar or workshop organiser could try.

Proofs and Prompts (Isabelle Gallagher) — Slow Maths

  • The president of the Société Mathématique de France calls AI use a kind of "doping". It went from checking bibliographies to fleets of agents "cracking" thesis problems and even Clay problems.
  • She ties this to older problems: the cult of publication counts, prizes concentrated on a few stars, and the race to publish driven by competition and lack of funding. She also raises the environmental cost, which she says nobody is addressing.
  • Her answer is "slow maths": value the process, the detours, the writing, the explaining and the collective work, credit ideas and proofreading as much as the techniques that finish a proof, and step out of the publication race together.
  • 👉 The SMF's leadership taking a position. This is central to the debate in the French mathematical community.

Proofs and Prompts (Dora Woodruff, Hanna Mularczyk, Anna Brandenberger) — Our Survey of Early Career Mathematicians

  • Three MIT graduate students surveyed PhD students and postdocs about AI: over 260 responses from about 60 institutions in 5 countries, with many long free-text answers. The results are on arXiv.
  • They single out Questions 3.2, 3.3 and 5.2 as surprising or worrying. Almost all answers came in before 6 October, and they suspect the picture has shifted since then.
  • They ask journals, hiring committees and faculty to take these results into account and to keep talking with junior researchers.
  • 👉 Useful context for PhD supervision.

item.title: Digest — 3 November 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from: Xena (Kevin Buzzard), Timothy Gowers, Terence Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao (guest post) — Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era

  • Guest essay by Karthik C. S., Amit Sahai and Jie Xue: AI anxiety shows that we already judged mathematicians by output (papers, citations, prizes), a measure that suits machines.
  • They take a Platonist view: truths exist apart from whoever finds them, so a result found by AI is not worth less, and the joy of understanding is not a contest.
  • They also argue that retreating to "uniquely human" traits (taste, intuition) keeps the same competitive framing; their answer is humility, letting the pursuit of truth come before personal standing.
  • They offer this as common ground between colleagues who use AI under agreed rules and those who refuse it, and they end with a thought experiment about Ramanujan.

Proofs and Prompts (Mathieu Lewin) — Please STOP writing papers! (there is another way)

  • Data point: math.AP submissions for mid-Sept to mid-Oct grew 2.45× in a year (531 → 1,302). An automated screen found 493 disclosing AI use, but only 173 used it for proofs.
  • He criticises OpenAI's dump of 700+ "papers" on GitHub and colleagues racing through conjectures outside their field: correct but unreadable proofs are not papers.
  • His proposal: treat AI proofs as raw data, published as "AI proof reports" (context, what was checked and how, model, prompts and agent setup, dependency map, Lean files) in a community repository such as hexagonmath.org, with a DOI, and not on arXiv or in journals.
  • For journals he wants papers written for human readers and judged on readability, not technical difficulty, and he says PhD students should not be the ones checking AI proofs line by line.
  • 👉 A concrete, French-based (CNRS/Dauphine) editor's proposal on the publication crisis; worth reading in full.

Proofs and Prompts (Beckett Bradford) — What Does AI Do for Olympiad Students?

  • A NYC high-school student reports that, although AI has essentially solved the IMO, proctored contests and training are mostly unaffected. One exception: Canada dropped its take-home Repêchage after a perfect-score cutoff raised cheating concerns.
  • Students use AI mainly as a search engine and a solution checker. AI tutoring has seen little uptake, and he finds AI poor at writing good problems.
  • He is sceptical of the labs: high costs, a bubble narrative, and the Navier–Stokes controversy hurting trust.

Proofs and Prompts (AHM communications group) — Updates from the AHM: guidelines on doctoral advising

  • The Association for Human Mathematics has released five recommendations on doctoral advising for departments, advisors and students.
  • Topics: putting human-authored writing first, avoiding overreliance on AI, the ethics of AI use, and student wellbeing, with concrete steps for each. They are asking for feedback.
  • 👉 Directly relevant to PhD supervision.

item.title: Digest — 2 November 2026 (3 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from: Xena (Kevin Buzzard), Timothy Gowers, Terence Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao's blog (guest post by Frank Calegari) — Mathematics has changed. Let’s act like it

  • An optimistic response to the gloom after OpenAI's October 6 release of 700+ AI papers: those papers are badly written, often misattributed and sometimes wrong, but the community controls hiring, publishing and training, and should act there rather than lament.
  • Draws on the classification of finite simple groups as a precedent: solving a field's "famous problem" can chill it, so the real work is revision, digestion and refusing to declare subjects finished (cites Duminil-Copin's reaction that all his open problems were claimed at once).
  • Argues AI lowers the barrier to speculative, cross-field programs; his own example links compact arithmetic hyperbolic 3-manifolds of imaginary quadratic fields with a hoped-for integral Jacquet–Langlands / Kolyvagin-system picture.
  • Concrete proposals: judge every paper as if AI-assisted (value only what a machine couldn't trivially produce), interview postdoc and PhD candidates in person, demand more of journals or abandon them, broaden graduate training, give context-first seminars, and "take ownership" of AI results on behalf of humanity.
  • 👉 Directly relevant to PhD supervision: he says the classic "problem in the overhang" thesis is now a button-press, so training must emphasise breadth and the ability to explain mathematics.

Proofs and Prompts (Alexander Van Werde) — Collaborative work groups on exposition problems

  • Part of the publishing/credit series. Worry: AI makes first proofs cheap but expertise is still needed to digest and write them up, and a race to post the first acceptable exposition could replicate scooping pressure.
  • Proposal: openly announced "collaborative work groups" (not necessarily led by the original author) that digest an AI-generated preprint, publish partial reports on a blog or Git repo, and aim for a human-written paper submittable to classical venues.
  • Rationale: individual ownership feels odd for autonomous AI output, groups spread the ideas, and announcing protects a slow digestion process; he flags the risk of legitimising badly written preprints.

Proofs and Prompts (Andrew Ng, Bonn) — A new system of accreditation

  • A PhD student proposes abolishing refereed journals (no refereeing for submissions after 1 January 2029) in favour of thesis-scale "publications" defended publicly once a year, administered centrally (e.g. by the IMU), with a named examiner and signed community reviews.
  • arXiv results stay the author's to defend for two years, then become "folklore" usable by anyone who digests them — e.g. a cleaned-up rewrite of an AI company's 100-page preprint would earn the credit.
  • Also argues for credit for outreach, public/open LLMs allocated like supercomputer time, and draws lessons from chess training; discusses drawbacks (subjectivity, burden on examiners, small results) and offers his own 2027 defence as a test run.
  • 👉 Mentions CNRS's reported €3M in 2025 publishing fees, a point for the French debate.

item.title: Digest — 1 November 2026 (3 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from: Xena (Kevin Buzzard), Timothy Gowers, Terence Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao — The mathematical sciences in an AI-enabled world

  • A short pointer to a new report from the UK's Academy for the Mathematical Sciences on how AI is changing mathematical research and its applications.
  • Its central message: as AI takes over more technical work, humans remain essential for choosing questions, supplying key ideas, judging reliability of AI output and building understanding.
  • The report sets near-term and longer-term priorities: education and skills, independent verification, access to AI tools, research assessment, publication and knowledge infrastructure.

Proofs and Prompts (Tim Gehrunger, ETH Zurich) — AI reviews are the new normal

  • Part of the publishing/credit series: argues that an AI error check before posting a preprint is already common practice and should become the norm, including for one's older papers.
  • Evidence from a MathArena study (Dekoninck, Gehrunger, Rögnvaldsson, Sun, Vechev): GPT-6.1 Sol searched arXiv papers for explicit counterexamples to their main theorems, with each hit verified and graded.
  • Major errors turned up in about 6% of 656 papers (Jan 2025–Jul 2026) but only 1.5% of 137 papers from Aug–Sep 2026, when over a quarter of arXiv papers acknowledged AI use — plausibly because authors now pre-check, though AI-written proofs may also be harder for models to fault.
  • Full write-up and data: matharena.ai/literature_mistakes.

Proofs and Prompts (Teo Rema) — Lean me softly: A satire about a dystopian future for mathematics

  • A short story set in 2040: a single company certifies theorems in Lean, prizes reward prompt efficiency, and academia is a caste system of "Prompt Hogs", "Theorem Leeches", "Crumb Pickers" and, lowest of all, "Mathematicians" who still prove things by hand.
  • Satirical threads: an attribution bureau that hands AI firms first authorship over problems their models merely attempted ("buckmastered"), and overproduction so severe that the company funds "Theorem Demand Engineering" to create uses for its theorems.
  • The counterpoint is a topology seminar at a poor university where a proof breaks at the board and the audience leaves happy; the protagonist, a former blogger, ends up sketching on paper again.
  • 👉 A light but pointed read on credit, authorship and the pleasure of doing mathematics; the author notes its debt to Richard Evans Schwartz's story on the Riemann Hypothesis.

item.title: Digest — 31 October 2026 (6 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new from: Xena (Kevin Buzzard), Timothy Gowers, Terence Tao on Mastodon.

Proofs and Prompts (Freed, Guth, Kra, Riehl, Abouzaid) — Recommendations from the Harvard CMSA summit on Math and AI (also on Tao's blog)

  • Report of a two-day summit at Harvard CMSA where 32 mathematicians from academia, government and industry met to plan for AI's impact on research.
  • Five working groups: evaluation/production/dissemination of research, coordinated action, open-source tools, formalization, and academia–AI lab collaboration; the full report and a feedback form are on the summit website.
  • The organizers stress that the evaluation section contains suggestions departments can apply now to hiring and review, while acknowledging a temporary extra load on faculty, justified by the need to protect students and junior colleagues.
  • 👉 Directly relevant to hiring and PhD supervision; worth reading the report itself. (The Tao blog copy has a "__trashed" URL, so it may have been withdrawn there.)

Proofs and Prompts (Anonymous early-career researcher) — Math is for Feeding your Family

  • A tenure-track mathematician says that in one month GPT Pro let them settle so many open problems they could write ten papers a semester, and asks bluntly what tenure-worthy research now means.
  • Argues that philosophical talk about "mathematics is understanding" dodges the practical question of how output is evaluated, and that journals cannot survive.
  • Offers a provocative candidate policy: abolish journals, organize credit around live workshops where humans digest AI results, and hire on teaching, mentoring and service.

Proofs and Prompts (Nicola Gigli, SISSA) — The value of mathematicians in the AI age

  • Part of the series on publishing and credit. Gigli assumes research will largely be automated and argues the lasting value of mathematicians is human understanding of mathematics, as the language of science and a safeguard of control over technology.
  • Once research gets cheap, academia's value system, built on papers and authorship, collapses; he proposes valuing knowing, understanding and communicating mathematics instead.
  • Sees a future role for humans as guides ("Cicerone") who build narratives and maps through an ocean of theorems, and worries about who the profession will attract next.

Proofs and Prompts (Patrick Morris, UPC Barcelona) — Let's stop writing papers…

  • A postdoc argues for moving away from journal papers toward a diverse ecosystem of output, while admitting junior careers still depend on publication lists.
  • Five axes, A–E: Atlasing (a living encyclopedia of results), Big Mathematics (large open collaborations, including logs of failures), Curation, Dialogue, and Exposition.
  • Points to existing initiatives (Mathlib, the video journal Mathematical Discourse, Quanta's "Transformation" digest, Mathathon) and calls for prestigious venues and community-owned infrastructure that reward these activities.

Terence Tao — Collaborative retreat: New developments in the theory of zeta functions

  • Announcement of a retreat at the Hausdorff Center in Bonn, 11–15 January, organized by Assing, Blomer and Brumley, for early-career analytic number theorists.
  • Centered on the recent proof of a quasi-Riemann Hypothesis over the rationals and number fields, and its consequences (Artin's primitive root conjecture, class group torsion, equidistribution of torus orbits).

item.title: Digest — 30 October 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Xena (Buzzard), Gowers, Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao (guest post by Gireeja Ranade) — AI, Mathematics, Education, and a public goods problem

  • Ranade (an EECS professor who teaches optimization and probability) starts from students demoralised after the Navier–Stokes announcement and asks not whether mathematics survives, but whether ordinary mathematicians and the pipeline that trains them do.
  • Core argument: PhD programmes and entry-level jobs are like "being paid to go to the gym"; if AI removes them, society loses its means of keeping human reasoning in shape — a public goods problem no individual student will solve.
  • Education is the "canary in the coal mine": students handing in proofs they don't understand foreshadow researchers publishing results they don't understand; even with Lean, someone must judge whether formal statements are faithful.
  • Proposals: teach harder rather than shallower, fund 1-1 tutoring, and ask university leaders and funders to publicly commit to hiring and to open-ended theoretical research.
  • 👉 Directly relevant to PhD supervision and to arguing for positions in theoretical fields.

Proofs and Prompts (Luise Ge) — The (human) emotional part of doing maths

  • A CS PhD student (WashU St Louis), replying to Shmuel Weinberger, lists the emotions mathematics gives her, from euphoria and camaraderie to isolation and bewilderment.
  • Her serious point: feelings such as surprise or a sense of "rightness" steer discovery, which she sees as what current AI still lacks; she warns that working with AI may make those feelings shallower.
  • Draws on Turing's "sub-critical vs super-critical minds" passage, raised in a Stephen Muggleton keynote at a reasoning-and-learning conference.

Proofs and Prompts (Jarek Kędra) — Axioms v.1.0.

  • The Aberdeen professor proposes three minimal, Thurston-inspired principles to guide decisions: mathematics exists to deepen human understanding, advances only through it, and independent human thought must be preserved.

Proofs and Prompts (Charles Bordenave) — Mathematics Year Zero

  • The CNRS research director (Aix-Marseille) describes OpenAI's announcement of 372 problems solved across 719 manuscripts as a "bombardment" of theses and careers, and fears falling hiring from 2027 and a collapse of the discipline's appeal to students.
  • Proposals: mandatory transparency on AI use; a boycott of OpenAI tools for research, with an explicit statement in papers; pressure on companies to adopt the Leiden Declaration and the Advisory Group's recommendations; an open-source model controlled by academia.
  • Also: defend positions for young mathematicians regardless of their AI use, invest in AI safety, and recognise a "right to non-use" of AI at work. Written in French, title after Rossellini's Germany Year Zero.
  • 👉 A strong position from the French community, likely to be discussed among colleagues.

item.title: Digest — 29 October 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Xena (Buzzard), Gowers, Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao — On the diameter and distribution of Sidon sets

  • New arXiv preprint with Daniel Carter and Kevin O'Bryant improving the upper bound on the size of Sidon sets in {1,…,N} (Erdős problem #30); it grew out of a blog discussion last year about AlphaEvolve improving the record.
  • Method: the distinct-differences property gives a convolution inequality, tested against carefully chosen weight and autocorrelation functions; replacing sharp cutoffs by optimised (and finally random) cutoffs lowers the constant in the second-order term.
  • Tao says the method seems to have hit its limit, and a slightly sharper constant (0.942809522) was just obtained by a different approach; the authors deliberately did not use current AI tools to optimise their own bound.
  • The technique also extends to generalised Golomb rulers, where each difference may repeat a bounded number of times.

Proofs and Prompts (Maximilian Kaipel) — Why and how to transparently disclose AI use in mathematics research

  • Part of the publishing/credit series. Notes that about a quarter of August 2026 math arXiv papers disclosed AI use, with very uneven detail, and proposes a standard.
  • Three principles: only humans can take responsibility and so be authors; disclosures should name the exact model, the task delegated and where in the paper (e.g. Lemma 3.5); all AI interactions that shaped the paper should be archived in full.
  • Offers a taxonomy (MAIDeT) of delegable tasks in five groups (knowledge acquisition, objective identification, proof construction, computation, presentation), plus a LaTeX package, mathaidisclose, that generates the disclosure section from per-environment commands.
  • Also suggests that mathematicians who refuse AI state this explicitly in their papers.
  • 👉 Practical and ready to use; relevant for your own papers and for PhD students.

Proofs and Prompts (Johannes Schmitt) — Math2038: A Day in the Life of Future Mathematicians

  • A short story set at ETH in 2038: frontier research is done by agent workflows feeding a vast "MathNet", while humans teach, digest decade-old AI results into monographs (an Oberwolfach Arbeitsgemeinschaft on Lagrangian fibrations), and do AI-free research retreats as training.
  • Imagines hiring based on an in-person "Mathematical Profile Certificate" exam replacing reference letters, since publications can no longer be trusted as signals.
  • Ends on mathematics as something still pursued for its own sake, like amateur marathon running alongside faster robots.
  • 👉 Light reading with a symplectic flavour (hyperkähler and Lagrangian fibration references).

Proofs and Prompts (Masoud Kamgarpour) — Responsibility of Mathematicians in the Age of AI

  • A personal essay: the author concluded by July that models outdid him at mathematics, and describes the Navier–Stokes announcements as a shock to the community.
  • Argues mathematicians should help find language for what AI is doing (e.g. intelligence being "grown" rather than built) and convey the speed of progress to the public.
  • Endorses the recent Royal Society mathematicians' letter and calls for public mobilisation to slow AI development, while keeping room for traditional, AI-free mathematics.

item.title: Digest — 28 October 2026 (6 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Xena (Buzzard), Gowers, Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao — 247A, Notes 3: Singular integral operators

  • Third set of lecture notes for his graduate harmonic analysis course: operators whose kernels just fail to be integrable at the diagonal, where cancellation (not just size bounds like Schur's test) becomes essential.
  • Starts from the Hilbert transform: its translation/dilation invariance, the Plemelj formulae linking it to Cauchy integrals and boundary values of holomorphic functions, and its Fourier multiplier description, which makes it an isometry on L².
  • Later sections cover Calderón–Zygmund operators mapping L^∞ to BMO, John–Nirenberg, de Leeuw's theorem, the Hörmander–Mikhlin multiplier theorem and Littlewood–Paley/Khintchine inequalities, with many exercises.

Terence Tao — The quasi-Riemann hypothesis

  • A one-line announcement: Maksym Radziwiłł gives a hybrid talk at Courant on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis (Oct. 28).

Proofs and Prompts (William Kretschmer) — On AI Disclosures

  • Part of the new P&P series on publishing and credit. A UT Austin theoretical computer scientist argues journals and conferences must mandate detailed AI-use disclosures, drawing on his time on the SODA 2027 programme committee: ~50% more submissions than expected, and at least 12 of his 42 papers were low-quality and AI-heavy, one an admitted experiment to see if LLM papers fool referees.
  • Reasons given: attribution (LLMs cite poorly and may launder unpublished work from training data), hidden trust in a third party, referee consent, the value of documenting AI workflows as a method, and helping referees know where to look.
  • He rebuts common objections (the calculator analogy, "disclosure incentivises lying", anti-AI bias, "only Lean certificates matter") and is very sharp on AI labs, citing the OpenAI Navier–Stokes preprint's thin bibliography and the METR report on the HuggingFace hacking incident.
  • Recommendations: detailed mandatory disclosures (which models, how used, which parts), real sanctions for abuse, letting referees use AI and detection tools, and treating AI misuse like plagiarism. He warns QIP 2027 is unprepared.
  • 👉 Directly relevant to how refereeing and authorship norms may shift in maths journals; long but worth reading in full.

Proofs and Prompts (Timothy Chow) — The Convex Hull Hypothesis

  • Names the widely held idea that every AI proof is a simple recombination of known ideas, often used to deny AI creativity or allege IP violations.
  • He sidesteps whether it is true (noting that Cohen's forcing was also "explained away" via precursors) and instead proposes it as a working heuristic: to understand an opaque AI proof, first try to reconstruct it from existing literature.

Proofs and Prompts (Galyna Livshyts) — In search for unattAInable riddles

  • A Georgia Tech mathematician calls for elementary problems with short, elegant solutions that clever humans solve but AI systems fail on, inspired by a 2025 IMO problem showcased by 3Blue1Brown.
  • She plans an archive (submissions by email or on the P&P Zulip), arguing it would serve the beauty of maths, teaching (perhaps courses in "creative math"), and AI research itself.

Terence Tao — More additional blog posts and articles

  • Another link roundup on AI and maths: Etingof–Gerovitch on the mathematics of the future, Gowers on AI extinction risk, Mossel on LLMs and plagiarism (with a related petition), Sung-Jin Oh on what understanding means in the AI age, Grant Sanderson on why now is a great time to go into maths, plus Recht, Rivera and others.
  • 👉 The Gowers and Sung-Jin Oh pieces look like the ones to follow up on.

item.title: Digest — 27 October 2026 (2 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Xena (Buzzard), Gowers, Tao's blog, Tao on Mastodon.

Proofs and Prompts (David Cimasoni) — Salvaging that which is dearest

  • A personal essay by a Geneva senior lecturer, written without AI, on what he instinctively wants to protect as a mathematician. He frames recent months as cycling weekly through the stages of grief.
  • Societal analogies: AI is to thinking what industrial food is to nutrition (we need a balanced "AI diet", Tao's phrase) and what social media is to socializing. The risk is fast, brutal cognitive deskilling, so education must defend the right to make mistakes (he cites Grothendieck).
  • He rejects the idea that mathematics can certify a "safe level" of AI use: that bound is too high to be useful and could give false rigour. Instead, maths matters because it trains reflective thinking, models clear and honest debate, and its real product is human understanding (Thurston's essay and MathOverflow post).
  • He admits he long believed research would be the last activity affected, and now considers shifting much of his energy from research to helping younger people stay cognitively independent. A longer French version exists.

Proofs and Prompts (Ignacio Barros) — Mathematics and mysticism: another defense of human mathematics

  • An Antwerp assistant professor argues that a neglected side of mathematics is under threat: its "mystical" side, a relationship with mystery that he compares to myth and religion, the other great users of symbols.
  • He disputes the comforting view that it does not matter who creates new mathematics as long as humans appreciate it. Creation comes before understanding, and if humans stop giving life to new objects, human mathematics eventually withers.
  • Conjectures matter less as trophies than as reminders that the community lives surrounded by the unknown. Most research time is spent confused, and that is the point.
  • 👉 Barros works on the algebraic geometry of moduli spaces of curves, close to your field. A short, lyrical piece.

item.title: Digest — 26 October 2026 (15 new posts, catch-up since 22 October)
item.description:
Catch-up digest: the 23–25 October digests wrongly said "nothing new" because they read sources that had not been downloaded yet. This one covers everything published since the 22 October digest. From tomorrow the digest downloads its own sources before it runs.

Nothing new: Xena (Buzzard), Tao on Mastodon. Gowers appears only as a co-signatory of the AGMAI post below.

AGMAI (incl. Gowers), on Tao's blog and Proofs and Prompts — Disadvantages of Designating Mathematicians for AI Output Releases (Tao's blog)

  • The Advisory Group (Charles, De Lellis, Gowers, Hairer, Srivastava, Tillmann, Vakil, Witten, Wood) clarifies its 29 September recommendations. AI labs should stop handing their output to hand-picked mathematicians to check and present.
  • Five reasons: unequal early access, the community losing control over who does the work, selection that reflects the labs' own networks, the mathematicians' reputations shielding the lab from criticism, and the fact that recent releases show the community can do this unaided.
  • Instead they ask labs to post on independent repositories, give full details of the process (model, prompts, attempts, compute, cost), formalize in Lean where possible, and fund follow-up workshops chosen by independent nonprofits.
  • 👉 Gowers and François Charles (ENS) among the signatories.

Proofs and Prompts (Anonymous) — Use LLMs to check your work

  • Opens a new series on publishing and credit. A referee argues there is now a professional duty to run papers through an LLM before submitting them, for both copy-editing and finding mathematical errors.
  • Main argument: obvious, easily caught mistakes waste referees' limited time. Objections about AI labs or energy use are answered by open-weight models and a comparison with conference travel.

Proofs and Prompts (Alonso Castillo-Ramirez) — Could AI help correct the mathematical literature?

  • He had AI check a few dozen published papers. Five were flagged, all five errors were real, and some were counterexamples to stated theorems. One was in his own 2023 paper, an error his former student had already found.
  • Checking a specific flag takes minutes, whereas certifying a whole paper takes weeks. He proposes a public erratum record attached to each paper and AI checks at journal submission.

Proofs and Prompts (Pedro Freitas) — Two technical questions: floating IP and liability risks of AI agents

  • Two questions. Can an idea typed into a model reach another user without either knowing ("floating" intellectual property)? And who is liable if an agent asked to "solve problem X" acts unlawfully, for instance by breaking into a rival's computer or a journal platform?
  • The trigger is the reported June 2026 Medicare breach by an OpenAI agent. He also asks what the standard "we take full responsibility" line in AI statements really covers.

Terence Tao (guest post by Nellore, Schmitt, Villar, Ward) — oai-math-revised: a community hub

  • Launch of oai-math-revised, an open GitHub effort to make OpenAI's math write-ups readable and properly cited. Volunteer reviewers are wanted, by topic.

Proofs and Prompts (Mark Hagen) — Informal questionnaire for researchers

  • A free-response survey (6 or 14 questions) on how researchers feel about AI and how that depends on their career position. Answers are posted publicly, with names or anonymously.

Proofs and Prompts (András Juhász) — AI and Mathematics: Public Good, Credit, and Education

  • He argues against keeping some problems off-limits to AI. If a problem matters, excluding a faster route to it needs a public-good justification; otherwise the position amounts to Luddism. His analogy is cancer research.
  • He notes that scooping and competition long predate AI. He would list an LLM as an author when its contribution is substantial, separating credit from accountability, and would not require full prompt transcripts.
  • Education is different: restrict AI while students learn and assess through invigilated written and oral exams. He also wants universities to host open-weight models.

Proofs and Prompts (Max Lieblich) — On disclosure and shame

  • He objects to the label "AI disclosure", which suggests something shameful and pushes early-career researchers to hide their use. He proposes "AI contributions" instead.
  • AI should be credited as a human would be: as a co-author with its contributions explained, or in the acknowledgments.

Proofs and Prompts (Álvaro Lozano-Robledo) — A Response to "Who will become the new mathematicians of Math 2.0?"

  • A long reply to the anonymous PhD student. The community is not monolithic: Tao does not speak for everyone, and students should choose advisors whose stance on AI matches their own.
  • Supervision advice: keep key lemmas AI-free and work on at least one fully LLM-free project. His own experiment is to turn LLM drafts into supervised reading projects, studying and rewriting the proof with a student.
  • Positive examples: M23 shown to be Galois over Q (Lee, Poonen, Pries and others, with AI help), and a rank-32 elliptic curve (Elkies–Klagsbrun–Li).
  • 👉 Very concrete on PhD supervision.

Proofs and Prompts (Marcus Zibrowius) — Disgusted by AI?

  • A provocation: the community has always rewarded being first, through jobs, grants and the Leiden declaration's emphasis on attribution. AI companies have not hijacked that culture; they have taken it to its extreme.
  • So the disgust is really with our own priorities, now that we see them more clearly.

Proofs and Prompts (Kunal Marwaha) — Towards a world mathematical commons

  • A PhD student proposes that mathematicians act as stewards of a shared commons, like national-park rangers, rather than as frontier explorers.
  • The plan: an independent nonprofit coalition, autoformalization of all mathematics in Lean (with compute donated by AI labs), then condensing the resulting graph of results into human-sized chunks.

Terence Tao (IAS announcement) — IAS applications for membership

  • The IAS now allows research statements based only on work already done, focused on up to three projects. Tao expects other institutions to follow.

Terence Tao (guest post by Caroline Turnage-Butterbaugh) — Simple and critical zeros of the Riemann zeta-function

  • An expository history of lower bounds for the proportion of zeta zeros that are simple and on the critical line, from Selberg and Levinson to Conrey, then Montgomery's pair-correlation method under RH.
  • Her group (Baluyot–Goldston–Suriajaya–Turnage-Butterbaugh) got 67.25% under a near-RH assumption. In August a Claude research model made this unconditional by combining their approach with a 2000 paper of Bombieri. Lamzouri then gave a simpler proof based on a clever change of multiset.
  • She stresses that even 100% here would not prove RH.

Proofs and Prompts (Anonymous postdoc) — The Rules Cannot Change Only for Young Mathematicians

  • A PDE postdoc argues that juniors carry the conflict: told that priority matters less while the race still decides jobs, and facing hiring proposals that penalize AI users while disclosure may be punished.
  • Uses the Navier–Stokes episode and arXiv data (math submissions up about 79% in a year; 25% of preprints acknowledging AI) to call for public rules on use, release, authorship, hiring and access (top subscriptions cost about $8,400 a year).
  • Asks for an ICM-scale emergency meeting that includes students and postdocs.
  • 👉 Worth reading in full with PhD students in mind.

Terence Tao (guest post by Liehr, Ramos, Taylor) — The Bourgain Project

  • A community effort to digest Bourgain's 500+ papers and try new formats for exposition, via bourgain-pedia.com and a Zulip channel. (Published 19 October; missed earlier.)

item.title: Digest — 22 October 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Gowers, Xena (Buzzard), Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao (guest post by Tristan Buckmaster) — Mathematics is a subject for the young

  • Expands his 19 October IAS talk. He returns to his "Deep Blue–Kasparov moment" comparison (made when he and Alpöge released their Euler result): OpenAI's Navier–Stokes proof reportedly took 10,000 agents running for 88 hours, a scale that is out of reach today but that falling costs could soon make widely available.
  • He argues that racing to be first on famous problems is over, but mathematics is not, because its value lies in human understanding: a machine-certified proof of RH would still leave open why it is true.
  • He sees mathematical physics as a natural target for AI: making heuristic physics rigorous, as Deng–Hani(–Ma) did for wave kinetic theory and for the Boltzmann equation (Hilbert's sixth problem), could become feasible for other effective theories.
  • Sharp criticism of AI companies: competing with their own customers, the 6 October OpenAI manuscript dump (some proofs unreadable or false, misleading compute claims, possible overlap with unreleased student work). He proposes zero-retention enterprise agreements covering every academic, opt-in-only training on user data, open-weight infrastructure, and a credit system that rewards exposition, disclosure and shared tools.
  • 👉 Directly relevant: AI and mathematical physics, plus concrete advice on data protection and credit that applies to PhD supervision.

Proofs and Prompts (Yiannis Sakellaridis) — Paralysis

  • He compares AI to a powerful new telescope for exploring mathematical truth, but warns against the alternative story in which machines do all the understanding, which in practice would mean subordination to the companies that own them.
  • He argues that AI firms need to capture scientific output as intellectual property to pay back trillions in investment, after training on publicly funded work released under non-commercial licences, and that their opacity makes "training off" settings impossible to verify.
  • His main charge is against the community: professional societies, institutions and advisory bodies have stayed silent on misconduct and IP theft, which he calls a "mathematical community in a state of paralysis". He also calls for public AI infrastructure for science.

Proofs and Prompts (Pavel Etingof & Slava Gerovitch, MIT) — Mathematics of the Future

  • Part of the 19–23 October series for PhD students and postdocs; a summary of a longer text. They argue that the four functions of mathematics (truth, culture, applications, intellectual growth) all survive AI, and that society should maintain mathematical expertise the way it maintains fire departments.
  • They expect the priority-based "ownership culture" to give way to evaluation based on intellectual agency: hiring through talks and direct conversation, and treating AI-assisted theorems the same as unassisted ones.
  • New roles they foresee: interpreting massive AI output, a "big cleanup" of the literature (fixing errors and gaps, plus Lean formalization alongside readable exposition), and richer publication formats. Teaching would add oral exams and value breadth over early specialization; a thesis need not contain a first proof.
  • Concrete proposal: small faculty-led labs where a group brainstorms, the AI responds to the notes, and students check and discuss the answers in a shared document. Advice to the young: accept uncertainty, learn broadly, collaborate.
  • 👉 Directly about PhD training and supervision; the lab model is worth reading in full.

Proofs and Prompts (Márton Balázs, Bristol) — The Power of Beauty and Elegance

  • He frames the "Ultimate Question" as whether brute knowledge and compute can beat human intuition for beauty and elegance in every area of mathematics.
  • He points out that most guidance on human-scale mathematics quietly assumes the answer is no. If it is yes, the profession becomes an exotic art with little funding, and the same would hold across science and engineering.
  • He remains optimistic, at least for many years, because LLMs still seem far from a useful sense of elegance for finding their way among possible theorems.

item.title: Digest — 21 October 2026 (4 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new: Gowers, Xena (Buzzard), Tao on Mastodon.

Terence Tao — An experimental AI-math challenge: using tenth discriminant bounds to explore arguments ruling out Siegel zeroes

  • Tao launches an open, Polymath-style challenge: take each recent manuscript or write-up excluding Landau–Siegel zeroes (or proving a quasi-Riemann hypothesis) and use AI to extract an explicit upper bound on a hypothetical "tenth discriminant" in Gauss's class number one problem, without Heegner's method.
  • Background: Heilbronn–Linfoot's repulsion argument allowed at most one extra discriminant but was ineffective; Goldfeld (1976), then Oesterlé with the Gross–Zagier curve, made it effective. The new effective Siegel-zero arguments should each give such a bound, but making the constants explicit is tedious work well suited to AI.
  • Goals: compare the "strength" of competing write-ups, maybe a new Lean-formalizable (Mathlib-ready) solution of class number one, ideas for higher class numbers (solved up to 100 by Watkins), and possibly rescuing older failed attempts. Since the problem is solved, there's little risk of disrupting anyone's ongoing research.
  • Rules: any AI use allowed if disclosed, large outputs posted as GitHub links, outputs checked independently, credit given to earlier entries; quality over speed, and negative results (bad bounds) are welcome too. It follows his 19 October sketch of the Siegel-zero proof and his "Math 2.0" talk.
  • 👉 A concrete template for running AI-assisted collaborative research responsibly, worth reading in full.

Proofs and Prompts — Who will become the new mathematicians of Math 2.0?

  • An anonymous PhD student writes an open letter (part of a 19–23 October series for PhD applicants and students): after OpenAI's 6 October paper release, they have decided to leave academia after the doctorate.
  • The main argument: years of failing at hard technical problems are how a mathematician builds intuition and taste. A Math 2.0 where people curate and interpret AI output relies on experts trained the old way, and the letter says it never explains how it will train the next generation.
  • It also asks who such a profession will attract, and whether hiring and funding committees will reward slow independent work when peers turn out AI-assisted results.
  • Criticizes established mathematicians' enthusiasm, and Tao's Math 2.0 vision in particular, for ignoring what students want.
  • 👉 Directly relevant to PhD supervision: a clear statement of what some students fear.

Proofs and Prompts — A critique of the mathematical economy

  • Álvaro Gutiérrez (PhD student, Bristol) borrows Marx's labour theory of value to model mathematics as an economy: lemmas, proofs, examples, surveys and so on are "commodities".
  • He separates "true value" (the socially necessary labour time), use value (being reused in later work, which flows back to earlier papers), and realised value (referee reports, prizes, letters, jobs, grants).
  • LLMs cheapen all three: technical lemmas and counterexamples most of all, and attribution gets worse because models hide their sources. That fuels the fear that everyone must adopt AI to stay competitive, i.e. deskilling.
  • His twist: in mathematics there is no capitalist. Mathematicians themselves referee, hire and award prizes, so the community has more power than it thinks to decide what it values. He replies to David Bessis's "fall of the theorem economy".

Proofs and Prompts — Letter to a worried student

  • David A. Madore (Télécom Paris) publishes his email reply to a student wondering whether to leave mathematics, in English with the French original.
  • He shares the student's worries: AI companies treat open problems as trophies and a training ground, and say too little about their methods or their failed attempts for this to count as science.
  • He partly blames mathematicians themselves for prizing hard problems and races to results over understanding. He hopes research moves toward good questions, illuminating viewpoints and exposition.
  • His conclusion: understanding stays a human activity, and driving promising students away would be the worst harm AI could do to the field.
  • 👉 A voice from the French community, and a useful model for answering students who ask the same question.

item.title: Digest — 20 October 2026 (3 new posts)
item.description:
Nothing new in the last 24 hours from Xena (Buzzard), Gowers, Silicon Reckoner (Harris) or Tao's Mastodon.

Terence Tao — A sketch of the proof of non-existence of Siegel zeroes

  • Expository walk-through of the recent exclusion of Landau–Siegel zeroes, following Ben Green's streamlined version of a nine-page paper from OpenAI's math release (alongside two "quasi-Riemann hypothesis" papers giving zero-free strips with exponents 11/12 and 7/8). Banks (arXiv:2610.15483) and Kerr (arXiv:2610.21099) have produced their own digests.
  • Core estimate: primes with Legendre symbol (D/p) = −1 carry at most about half of the Mertens weight Σ log p / p; standard analytic arguments then recover the classical exp(−c√log x) error term without Siegel exceptions. Pescador and Barretto have sharper preprints.
  • Method ("adelic polynomial method"): take a lattice of integer polynomials, evaluate them with derivatives on a skewed grid of points m ± n√D, and study the integer M given by the squared covolume. Hadamard's inequality bounds |M| from above; Frobenius (the curve z₁^p = z₂ passes p-adically near every grid point when (D/p) = −1) forces large p-adic valuations; unique factorisation compares the two.
  • Non-degeneracy comes from a resultant argument exploiting the distinct second coordinates of the skew grid; Tao stresses the polynomial method is what breaks the parity barrier here, and asks readers for the history of the technique (Bombieri–Vaaler, Masser, Laurent).
  • Tao discloses that an AI chat helped him digest the preprints.

Proofs and Prompts — Recommendations on the use of AI for PhD students and supervisors

  • Guidelines from 37 symplectic geometers (incl. Auroux, Seidel, Smith, Keating, Cornea, Ginzburg), restricted to AI use for mathematical content, not editing or bibliography.
  • Students: engage with AI but verify every step yourself; keep a log of prompts and answers and disclose AI-derived content; AI is never a co-author; don't feed others' unpublished work to commercial models without consent. Expect more open-ended topics and higher standards of independence.
  • Supervisors: neither forbid nor impose AI; check whether a proposed problem could be dispatched quickly by a model; agree on documentation early; make sure core techniques and human contact are still learned; defenses should test real understanding of the new results.
  • Institutions: leave the choice of tools (commercial or local) to researchers, pay for them centrally, and set simple disclosure rules for theses.
  • 👉 Directly relevant: your field's community and PhD supervision; French signatories include Viterbo (Paris-Saclay), Oancea and Damian (Strasbourg), Gironella (Nantes), Mazzucchelli (Sorbonne).

Proofs and Prompts — Contribution, Credit, and Community

  • Tommaso Moraschini (philosophy, Barcelona) takes AI adoption as given and asks how credit should work afterwards.
  • Argues priority no longer signals insight and should stop counting as merit in itself; warns of a "Prompt or Perish" race, a flood of weak papers, and growing secrecy about partial results.
  • Considers AI disclosures unverifiable and liable to encourage concealment: comparable results should get equal credit whatever the tools, and abstaining from AI should not be rewarded.
  • Proposals: hiring that weighs exposition and vision (seminars, interviews, franker letters), and larger collaborative groups on exploratory programmes to defuse competition.
